Leo Frank's Manufactured Murderer: The Attempt to Frame Newt Lee

Newt Lee at the Coroner's Inquest | The Atlanta Journal | Friday, May 9, 1913 | Atlanta, Georgia

The Night Watchman Who Became a Murder Suspect

On Friday, May 9, 1913, The Atlanta Journal published detailed accounts of the final coroner's inquest into the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan. Among the principal witnesses was Newt Lee, the Black night watchman who discovered her body in the basement of the National Pencil Company factory at 37 to 41 South Forsyth Street early Sunday, April 27.

Lee had telephoned police and led officers to the body. Yet within days, the man who reported the murder became a suspect, facing three pieces of potentially incriminating evidence: a disputed time-clock record, a blood-soaked shirt discovered at his residence, and two handwritten murder notes that appeared to point toward a Black man associated with the factory's night watch.

These objects later became central to the prosecution's argument that factory superintendent Leo Max Frank attempted to frame Lee. Particularly suspicious was Frank's changing account of the time slip, which he initially described as satisfactory before identifying gaps that supposedly gave the watchman enough time to travel home and return.

The May 9 Journal documented Lee's testimony, the detectives' findings, and serious questions about the conduct of Frank and his legal defense team (AJ, 6).

The Coroner's Inquest at Atlanta Police Headquarters

Fulton County Coroner Paul Donehoo conducted the inquest. His six-man jury initially assembled on Monday, April 28, at P. J. Bloomfield's undertaking establishment on South Pryor Street.

Later testimony was heard behind closed doors in the office of the Board of Police Commissioners at Atlanta police headquarters. The final session took place Thursday, May 8.

The jurors were foreman Homer C. Ashford, L. Glenn Dewberry, J. C. Hood, Clarence A. Langford, John Miller, and C. Y. Sheats.

Principal witnesses included Newt Lee, Leo Frank, Pinkerton investigator Harry Scott, city detective John R. Black, and factory official Herbert Schiff. Other leading figures included Chief of Detectives Newport Alonzo Lanford, Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey, and Frank's attorneys Luther Zeigler Rosser and Herbert J. Haas.

Lee was questioned about his movements on April 26, his conversations with Frank, the factory time clock, and the bloody shirt discovered at his residence. He continued to deny involvement in Mary Phagan's murder (AJ, 6).

Frank Orders Lee to Arrive Two Hours Early

Lee ordinarily began work at 6 p.m. On Friday, April 25, Frank instructed him to report at 4 p.m. the following afternoon, Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday.

When Lee arrived Saturday, he found the street entrance unlocked but the interior double doors locked, an unusual condition. Frank emerged from his private office, rubbing his hands, and unexpectedly told Lee to leave until 6 p.m.

Lee complained that he needed sleep, but Frank encouraged him to go out and enjoy himself.

Why would Frank instruct Lee to arrive two hours early, only to send him away?

One theory is that Frank wanted the watchman absent from the building. The defense could argue that Frank had simply changed his plans, but Lee's testimony established that his two-hour absence resulted from his employer's instructions (AJ, 6).

First Piece of Evidence: The Time Card

Saturday: Frank Handles the Clock

When Lee returned shortly before 6 p.m., Frank stopped him from punching the mechanical time clock while he installed a new paper recording slip.

The clock registered the watchman's rounds at approximately half-hour intervals. A complete record would support Lee's account of remaining on duty. Missing punches could suggest unexplained absences.

Frank's access to the mechanism became significant when the record was subsequently used against Lee (AJ, 6).

Sunday: Frank Says the Time Slip Is All Right

After Lee discovered Mary Phagan's body, police returned to the factory with Frank.

Frank opened the time clock and examined Lee's recording slip. William W. Rogers, known as Boots Rogers, also inspected it.

According to Rogers's testimony, Frank reported that the punches appeared satisfactory. Rogers likewise recalled seeing a punch corresponding to every numbered position.

Frank then installed another slip. The original record was not immediately secured under uninterrupted police custody.

The first inspection appeared to support Lee's account that he had made his rounds throughout the night (AJ, May 8, 1).

Monday: Frank Reports Missing Punches

By Monday, April 28, Frank was reporting discrepancies involving several missed half-hour punches.

One apparent gap extended from approximately 9:32 to 10:29 p.m. Other irregularities appeared around 11 p.m. and between approximately 2 and 3 a.m.

On Sunday, Frank said Lee's time slip was all right. By Monday, he was identifying missing punches that could implicate the watchman.

Frank explained that the first inspection had been superficial and that he had checked for marks without calculating every interval.

However, Lee insisted he had made his rounds regularly, and the handling of the original paper remained disputed.

No witness directly established that Frank altered the record, but the reversal in its interpretation created an opportunity to direct suspicion toward Lee (AJ, May 8, 1; AJ, July 31).

Frank Says Lee Had Time to Go Home and Return

During Frank's trial on Thursday, July 31, Detective John R. Black testified that Frank had remarked that the gaps in Lee's time record gave him sufficient time to leave the factory, travel home, and return during the night.

This statement connected the disputed time slip with the subsequent search of Lee's residence.

If investigators accepted the missing punches as evidence that Lee had abandoned his duties, they could argue that he went home to change bloodstained clothing before returning to the factory.

Under questioning by Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey, Black testified that police searched Lee's residence after Frank directed attention to the discrepancies.

Frank's attorney Luther Zeigler Rosser challenged Black's recollection and exposed uncertainty about the timing of several conversations. Nevertheless, Black maintained that Frank's statements concerning the time record had influenced the investigation of Lee (AJ, July 31).

Second Piece of Evidence: The Blood-Soaked Shirt

Detectives Search Lee's Residence

On Tuesday, April 29, Detectives John R. Black and Fred Bullard searched Lee's residence at 40 Henry Street.

At the May 8 coroner's inquest, Black testified that they discovered a heavily bloodstained shirt near the bottom of a clothes barrel, covered by discarded garments.

The shirt differed from the clothing Lee wore when police first encountered him.

Lee could not positively identify it. He explained that a woman had made several shirts for him and that, if the bloody garment was store-bought, it was not one of those shirts.

Pinkerton investigator Harry Scott testified that Lee said he had not worn the garment for approximately two years.

No witness established that Lee wore it during Mary Phagan's murder (AJ, May 9, 6).

The Laboratory Examination Raises Doubts

Atlanta city bacteriologist Dr. Claude A. Smith examined the shirt.

The Atlanta Journal reported on Thursday, May 8, that the stains appeared relatively recent and probably consisted of human blood.

But Smith's findings suggested that the shirt had not been worn since being washed. The blood appeared to have been deposited while the garment was unworn, possibly by applying blood to it or using it to wipe up blood.

This weakened the theory that Lee had worn the shirt during the killing.

Smith could not identify who deposited the blood or placed the garment in the barrel. Nevertheless, his findings raised the possibility that someone had deliberately stained the shirt and planted it among Lee's discarded clothing (AJ, May 8, 8–9).

Herbert Haas Demands a Search of Frank's Home

Frank's attorney Herbert J. Haas became another figure in the prosecution's attempted-frame-up argument.

During the July 31 trial, Detective Black testified that Frank arrived at police headquarters on Monday, April 28, and consulted with Haas and Luther Zeigler Rosser.

At approximately 11:30 a.m., Haas insisted that Chief of Detectives Newport Alonzo Lanford arrange a search of Frank's residence, with Frank accompanying the officers.

Black testified that Haas identified himself as Frank's attorney and insisted that investigators leave nothing undone to clear his client.

The demand appeared cooperative, but prosecutors questioned its purpose.

The search occurred two days after Mary Phagan's murder. Frank had therefore had time in which incriminating material could have been removed, washed, or discarded. A search finding nothing suspicious would strengthen the appearance of his cooperation.

The prosecution argued that the next step was to direct investigators toward Lee's residence, where the bloodstained shirt was discovered.

Dorsey explicitly declared:

"Our contention is that this shirt was a plant."

He argued that the search of Frank's home was part of a plan to redirect police suspicion toward Lee.

The allegation did not establish that Haas knew the shirt had been planted or that Frank personally placed it in the barrel, but the timing and order of the searches were central to the prosecution's theory (AJ, July 31).

Haas Attempts to Control the Pinkerton Reports

The May 9 Atlanta Journal reported another incident involving Haas.

Pinkerton investigator Harry Scott testified that Frank hired the agency on behalf of the National Pencil Company on Monday, April 28, supposedly to identify Mary Phagan's murderer.

According to Scott, Haas later asked him and Pinkerton superintendent Pierce to withhold their investigative findings from police until Haas had reviewed them.

Scott and Pierce refused, maintaining that they would rather withdraw from the investigation than accept the restriction.

The contrast was striking. Haas insisted that police search Frank's home while separately seeking to examine the private detectives' findings before those findings reached investigators.

An attorney may seek information for a client's defense, but attempting to control the reporting of evidence raised legitimate questions about the independence of an investigation conducted while the attorney's client was under suspicion (AJ, May 9, 6).

Third Piece of Evidence: The Murder Notes

Two handwritten notes were discovered near Mary Phagan's body early Sunday morning, April 27.

The messages contained unusual spelling and grammar and referred to a Black man and the night watchman.

Their wording threatened to direct suspicion toward Lee.

On April 29, The Atlanta Journal reported that three handwriting examiners believed Lee had written the notes.

Their opinions initially strengthened suspicion against him, although the comparisons did not conclusively establish authorship (AJ, April 29, 1).

James Conley Admits Writing the Notes

The investigation changed when National Pencil Company sweeper James Conley admitted writing the notes.

Conley initially gave conflicting accounts of their origin. By late May, he accused Frank of instructing him to prepare them.

During Frank's trial on Monday, August 4, Conley testified that Frank had supplied the writing materials and dictated the messages.

Frank denied the accusation, and the defense challenged Conley's credibility.

Conley's admission established that the notes were fabricated. Whether Frank directed their creation remained disputed.

If Conley's accusation was truthful, the notes were part of an effort to create false evidence that could implicate the night watchman (AJ, August 4).

Frank Confronts Lee at Police Headquarters

One of the most revealing portions of the May 9 Journal concerned a private conversation between Frank and Lee.

Detectives Harry Scott and John R. Black asked Frank to speak with Lee because they suspected the watchman knew more about the murder than he had disclosed.

Lee was handcuffed to a chair when Frank entered.

According to Lee, he complained about being detained for a crime he had not committed.

Frank replied that he believed Lee was innocent but thought he possessed information about the murder. The defense would keep this narrative going throughout the entire trial to create doubt.

Lee attempted to explain that he had patrolled the second floor every half hour and would have noticed something unusual if the killing occurred there during his rounds.

According to Lee, Frank interrupted and scolded him:

"Let's don't talk about that. Let that go."

The exchange raised questions about Frank's intentions. 

The interview was supposedly intended to obtain information, yet Frank allegedly discouraged Lee from explaining his movements.

Scott testified that Lee afterward complained that Frank had not genuinely attempted to obtain the truth.

Frank disputed the implication that he had tried to silence the watchman (AJ, May 9, 6).

The Coroner's Jury Holds Both Men

The coroner's jury concluded its investigation at approximately 6:30 p.m. Thursday, May 8.

The jurors determined that Mary Phagan died from strangulation and recommended holding both Frank and Lee for investigation by the Fulton County grand jury.

Deputy Sheriff Plennie Minor delivered the news at the Fulton County jail.

Frank was reading a newspaper and indicated that he expected the decision. He showed no emotions. It was an odd thing for a supposedly innocent man to act that way.

Lee appeared depressed and lowered his head dejectedly.

Neither Scott nor Black claimed to possess conclusive evidence identifying the murderer when the inquest ended (AJ, 6).

The Prosecution's Theory: Manufacturing a Murderer

The prosecution later argued that the three pieces of evidence were intended to work together.

The time slip would suggest that Lee had abandoned his duties.

The blood-soaked shirt would appear to explain the missing time as a trip home to change clothing.

The murder notes would direct suspicion toward a Black man associated with the factory's night watch.

Frank's changing interpretation of the clock record was central to that argument.

On Sunday, he reportedly declared the punches satisfactory. On Monday, he identified discrepancies.

Detective Black later testified that Frank suggested those gaps gave Lee time to travel home and return, and that the remarks influenced the search of Lee's residence.

The bloody shirt found there appeared to have been stained while unworn. Conley later admitted writing the murder notes and accused Frank of dictating them.

During the August closing arguments, Assistant Solicitor General Frank Arthur Hooper accused Frank of attempting to sacrifice the watchman to protect himself.

The allegation rested upon circumstantial evidence and disputed testimony. No eyewitness established that Frank personally altered the time slip or planted the shirt (AC, August 22, 2).

Conclusion: The Attempt to Frame Newt Lee

The May 9, 1913, Atlanta Journal documents how Newt Lee, the night watchman who reported Mary Phagan's murder, became a suspect under circumstances that deserved serious scrutiny.

Lee described Frank's unusual instructions, his handling of the time clock nervously (a foreshadowing?), and their private confrontation at police headquarters.

The subsequent investigation exposed a troubling pattern.

Sunday to Monday to Tuesday

Frank reportedly described Lee's time slip as satisfactory on Sunday, then identified missing punches on Monday. Detective Black later testified that Frank suggested those gaps gave Lee enough time to go home and return, after which police searched Lee's residence.

The bloodstained shirt discovered there on Tuesday appeared to have been stained while unworn. 

Conley subsequently admitted writing the murder notes and accused Frank of dictating them. Conley stated the purpose of the notes was to frame Newt Lee. 

Herbert Haas's involvement raised additional questions. He demanded that police search Frank's home while separately seeking to "review" Pinkerton findings before they reached investigators.

The prosecution argued that these circumstances revealed an attempt to manufacture evidence against Lee. It was a logical inference. 

The defense disputed that interpretation, and the surviving record does not conclusively establish Frank's personal responsibility for altering the time slip or planting the shirt.

Nevertheless, the contradictions in the time-clock testimony, the suspicious condition of the shirt, the fabricated murder notes, and the conduct of Frank's defense team formed the basis of the prosecution's argument that Frank attempted to make Newt Lee responsible for Mary Phagan's murder.

$OSCR KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM OSCAR HEALTH’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Oscar Health’s results indicate improving economics for well-positioned ACA insurers, not a uniformly improving healthcare environment. The combination of approximately 14% planned premium increases, favorable underwriting experience, competitor withdrawals, and administrative leverage supports selective insurer earnings recovery. Simultaneously, continued eligibility enforcement, coverage interruptions, and tighter medical management create pressure on hospital reimbursement and enrollment economics. The most actionable distinction is between companies retaining more premium through repricing and those absorbing the financial consequences when patients lose coverage. Oscar’s $250 million favorable risk adjustment revision is company-specific and should not be extrapolated across competing insurers. The strongest positive external implications concern Centene’s marketplace recovery, Allstate’s directly identified supplemental-insurance distribution opportunity, and eHealth’s employer-funded individual coverage channel. The strongest negative implications concern hospital payer mix and the continuing cost of verifying and retaining eligible ACA enrollment. Several supporting peer disclosures preceded Oscar’s call; the incremental information is corroboration and improved visibility, not a newly announced earnings event.

HOSPITALS AND ACUTE-CARE PROVIDERS

IMPROVING INSURER PROFITS DO NOT SIGNAL IMPROVING HOSPITAL PAYER MIX (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: HCA Healthcare (HCA: United States) and Community Health Systems (CYH: United States). Direction: negative for reimbursement quality, elective procedure mix, and cash conversion. Magnitude: material operating exposure for HCA and particularly consequential for Community Health Systems’ financially constrained equity. Oscar’s call strengthens an existing earnings-risk assessment rather than establishing an additional quantified hospital earnings reduction.

Call evidence: Oscar’s membership declined sequentially because of CMS eligibility reviews, with further disenrollments expected in Q4 and year-end membership projected at approximately 2.5 million, versus 2.69 million at September 30. Management expects additional verification measures to prevent some 2026 members from continuing into 2027. Bertolini also rejected an imminent subsidy rescue as a planning assumption: “right now, I don’t know that much of anything’s going to happen over the next year, at least.”

The transmission mechanism is loss of reimbursement rather than an equivalent disappearance of healthcare demand. Individuals losing exchange coverage can continue using emergency departments and receiving medically necessary treatment, but hospitals collect less revenue for those encounters. Elective procedures can simultaneously weaken because uninsured or underinsured patients delay treatment. The resulting combination is adverse: continuing labor and facility costs, lower collections, and reduced contribution from commercially reimbursed procedures.

HCA’s October 27 call independently demonstrated this mechanism. Management reported that patients losing exchange coverage were migrating almost directly into uninsured status, with that migration accounting for approximately 80% of uninsured volume growth. Uninsured equivalent admissions increased to approximately 10.5% of the total, versus 8.5% a year earlier. HCA estimated a roughly $400 million quarterly adjusted EBITDA headwind from exchange-to-uninsured payer-mix changes. That amount is HCA’s previously disclosed experience, not an incremental loss attributable to Oscar.

Community Health Systems’ October 29 commentary showed similar economic deterioration beneath growing patient volumes. Approximately half of its 3.6% same-store adjusted admission growth came from uninsured patients. Same-store revenue per adjusted admission increased only 0.2%, and management described declining collections on self-pay balances. This is an important warning against treating positive hospital volume growth as an adequate earnings indicator. Community Health Systems’ expected annual cash interest burden of approximately $800 million-$810 million further increases the importance of retaining operating cash flow.

Oscar’s description of removed members as primarily “non-utilizers” does not invalidate the hospital evidence. The companies observe different populations, periods, and treatment settings. Low utilization while enrolled with a particular insurer does not establish that an individual will generate no subsequent emergency care after losing coverage.

Near-term catalysts are Q4 payer-mix disclosures, cash collection trends, elective procedure volumes, and 2027 hospital guidance. The longer-duration concern is persistent coverage friction without enhanced subsidy restoration. Stable aggregate ACA enrollment would not automatically reverse hospital mix deterioration because replacement enrollment can differ geographically and demographically from the population losing coverage. Across portfolios, insurer and hospital holdings should not be treated as natural offsets: coverage disruption can worsen hospital collections and insurer risk selection simultaneously, even when insurer repricing temporarily produces stronger earnings.

MANAGED CARE AND ACA INSURANCE

PRICING DISCIPLINE SUPPORTS CENTENE’S MARKETPLACE RECOVERY, BUT NOT A SECTOR-WIDE RISK ADJUSTMENT WINDFALL (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Centene Corporation (CNC: United States), through Ambetter. Direction: positive for the durability of marketplace underwriting recovery. Magnitude: potentially material to consolidated earnings, although materially less direct than for Oscar because Centene also has large Medicaid and Medicare businesses.

Call evidence: Oscar plans approximately 14% weighted-average premium increases for 2027, incorporating medical trend, additional morbidity, and margin expansion. Blackley stated, “we also have built in a little bit of margin expansion in the pricing.” Management also identified approximately 850,000 lives displaced by competitor exits and expects overall marketplace enrollment to stabilize relative to year-end 2026.

The transmission mechanism is improved premium adequacy in a market where some competitors are withdrawing rather than maintaining uneconomic enrollment. An insurer with relevant networks and distribution can retain or acquire members at premiums that better reflect medical costs. Stable industry enrollment would also reduce uncertainty around the scale of the insured pool relative to another year of substantial contraction. These factors support underwriting recovery even without renewed industry membership growth.

Centene’s October 27 results provide direct corroboration. The company attributed improved marketplace health benefits performance to better pricing and risk transfers reflecting member acuity. Its commercial segment, which includes marketplace coverage, generated $8.7 billion of quarterly premium and service revenue, approximately 19% of the consolidated total. Marketplace membership was 3.40 million. The exposure is sufficiently large for modest underwriting changes to matter at group level.

For scale, a 100-basis-point improvement on an illustrative $10 billion of annual net premium revenue produces approximately $100 million of pretax underwriting benefit before associated expense changes. At Centene’s approximately 498 million diluted shares and roughly 26% adjusted tax-rate framework, that would represent approximately $0.15 per share. This is a sensitivity, not an estimate revision or an assumption about the size of Centene’s marketplace premium base.

Competitive withdrawals do not make share gains automatic. Oscar is expanding its own footprint by 24%, and Centene’s marketplace membership was substantially below the prior year. Ambetter announced additions in 55 counties for 2027, but it is also exiting Delaware and New Hampshire. Gross county additions therefore should not be interpreted as equivalent net geographic growth. The favorable conclusion concerns pricing and portfolio discipline, not an assured return to aggressive membership expansion.

The crucial limitation is risk adjustment. Oscar’s $250 million benefit does not establish that Centene should recognize a comparable revision. Transfers depend on relative risk within applicable markets, and competitors can experience different outcomes. The transferable positive evidence is improved pricing adequacy and market participation discipline. The company-specific transfer revision is not a shared profit pool.

Near-term catalysts are effectuated enrollment, local premium positioning, and Centene’s formal 2027 margin assumptions. The longer-duration positive is a more concentrated marketplace favoring insurers capable of combining underwriting discipline, local networks, and scalable administration. Oscar’s call adds confidence to that mechanism; it does not independently resolve Centene’s Medicaid or Medicare earnings trajectory.

ELIGIBILITY ENFORCEMENT REMAINS AN EARNINGS-VOLATILITY HEADWIND AFTER THE 2027 REPRICING BENEFIT (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected company: Centene Corporation (CNC: United States), particularly Ambetter. Direction: negative for enrollment retention, administrative cost, and underwriting predictability. Magnitude: potentially material within marketplace operations, with consolidated impact dependent on pricing offsets and the eventual implementation of proposed rules. This longer-duration risk qualifies, rather than contradicts, the near-term pricing recovery.

Call evidence: Oscar expects additional program-integrity measures and acknowledged that recent removals have been “mainly non-utilizers.” Management also described a moderation in favorable risk-pool evidence, from more favorable earlier reports to only moderately favorable recent information. Bertolini identified fragmented eligibility responsibilities between CMS and insurers as an operational problem requiring continuing data reconciliation.

The transmission mechanism has 3 components. Removing relatively low-utilizing members can increase average claims among those remaining. Verification requirements can also interrupt coverage for eligible individuals, reducing premium-paying member months without proportionately eliminating administrative work. Finally, brokers and insurers must spend more time resolving eligibility, consent, income, and documentation issues. The result can be simultaneous pressure on risk mix, acquisition expense, and retention.

Pricing can absorb anticipated deterioration, but it cannot eliminate uncertainty around which members leave. Stable total marketplace enrollment is not sufficient protection: newly enrolled members can differ from departing members in morbidity, geography, benefit selection, and acquisition cost. Similarly, a favorable current transfer estimate does not guarantee that subsequent market-risk information will remain favorable.

The October 23 CMS proposal creates a distinct 2028 exposure. It would require verification of specified eligibility criteria before financial assistance is provided and annual confirmation and reverification for subsidized automatic renewal. Members failing to complete the process could be renewed without financial assistance, rather than simply losing the possibility of automatic enrollment. For subsidy-dependent households, however, that distinction may offer little practical protection against coverage loss.

The proposed initial pre-enrollment verification window would begin August 1, 2027, for 2028 coverage. Consequently, spending on systems, outreach, broker support, and member retention could increase during 2027 before the full coverage effect becomes visible in 2028. The proposal’s implementation details remain subject to change; the negative mechanism is clear, but a specific earnings reduction is not yet supportable.

Near-term trading catalysts are rule finalization, subsequent enrollment integrity announcements, and revised insurer assumptions about membership and morbidity. The longer-duration fundamental issue is that ACA administration increasingly involves recurring verification and retention work rather than passive annual renewal. Larger insurers may gain relative share because they can support that infrastructure, but relative competitive advantage does not mean the absolute cost burden disappears.

SUPPLEMENTAL HEALTH INSURANCE

OSCAR PROVIDES A DIRECT DISTRIBUTION CHANNEL FOR ALLSTATE’S INDIVIDUAL SUPPLEMENTAL PRODUCTS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: The Allstate Corporation (ALL: United States), through Allstate Health Solutions. Direction: positive for supplemental policy distribution and premium generation. Magnitude: low at the consolidated Allstate level, but commercially relevant to the individual supplemental-health business. The call does not support a material group EPS upgrade.

Call evidence: Bertolini stated that the partnership “pairs Oscar plans with low-cost supplemental coverage to help bronze members manage out-of-pocket costs.” He also explained that Lucie can connect consumers to supplemental protection rather than requiring them to move to a richer ACA plan. Oscar’s October 20 product announcement identifies Florida and Texas as the initial markets and states that supplemental cash-pay options can accompany any Oscar plan there.

The transmission mechanism is targeted cross-selling at the point when consumers are choosing insurance and confronting deductibles. Oscar and Lucie provide access to shoppers already expressing a healthcare coverage need. Allstate Health Solutions can offer accident, serious-illness, or hospital-stay protection alongside the primary medical policy. This can create incremental policy sales through a distribution relationship rather than relying exclusively on separately acquired consumer leads.

The opportunity is more specific than a generic favorable read-through to supplemental insurers. Allstate Health Solutions is the named counterparty. No equivalent Oscar distribution relationship was identified for other listed supplemental carriers, so the same benefit should not automatically be assigned to them.

The product and ownership perimeter also matter. The partnership concerns individual supplemental coverage, not the employer stop-loss business sold to Nationwide or the separate employee voluntary-benefits business. Treating every historical Allstate health business as the beneficiary would misidentify the economic exposure.

Magnitude is constrained by geography, optional attachment, product premiums, commissions, and claims experience. Oscar’s 2.7 million members are not automatically Allstate customers, and Lucie’s approximately 800,000 projected new policies are neither entirely Allstate products nor entirely incremental insured individuals. No attachment rate, partner revenue split, or underwriting margin was disclosed. Allstate’s approximately $2.5 billion of Q3 adjusted net income also illustrates why a successful supplemental channel could remain small at group level.

The near-term catalyst is attachment during the current enrollment period, although separate public disclosure is not assured. The longer-duration opportunity is repeatable distribution of supplemental protection alongside high-deductible coverage. The partnership was announced before the earnings call; the call reinforced its strategic role rather than announcing a new award. These products also should not be assumed to reproduce the comprehensive benefits of a richer ACA plan or fully protect hospitals from unpaid patient obligations.

EMPLOYER BENEFITS AND DIGITAL INSURANCE DISTRIBUTION

CHOICE ADOPTION CREATES A FEE OPPORTUNITY FOR EHEALTH WITHOUT REQUIRING INSURANCE UNDERWRITING RISK (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: eHealth, Inc. (EHTH: United States). Direction: positive for its employer-funded individual coverage distribution opportunity. Magnitude: low demonstrated near-term contribution, with potentially meaningful longer-duration value if employer access converts into enrolled employees. The evidence supports the commercial mechanism, not an immediate consolidated earnings upgrade or an unconditional equity recommendation.

Call evidence: Oscar reported that CHOICE adoption is growing fastest across healthcare, technology, construction, and manufacturing in its operating states. The company is expanding employer-oriented products, extending Hy-Vee Health with Oscar into additional states, and introducing HelloMeno off-exchange. These are indications that employer-funded individual coverage is moving beyond a policy concept into product and distribution activity.

The transmission mechanism differs from the insurer opportunity. When an employer contributes a defined amount toward individually selected coverage, an intermediary can earn fees for administering the arrangement and commissions for placing employee policies. It need not retain the medical underwriting risk associated with those policies. Employer migration can therefore expand fee revenue even when participating insurers experience volatile risk adjustment or claims.

eHealth’s November 4 call establishes a concrete route to that opportunity. Its BerniePortal partnership is intended to give more than 5,000 employers and 1,000 insurance brokers access to eHealth’s CHOICE evaluation and coverage-selection capabilities. Management described the economics as a per-employee monthly administration charge plus broker commission. Oscar’s commentary independently supports demand for the underlying arrangement, rather than merely repeating eHealth’s own market-development expectations.

The distribution figures describe potential access, not contracted enrollment or guaranteed revenue. For scale, every 10,000 active employees would generate $120,000 of annual administration revenue for each $1 of monthly per-employee fees, before placement commissions and servicing costs. Actual pricing and enrolled employee counts were not disclosed, so a more precise revenue estimate would be speculative.

Lucie is an important competitive qualification. Oscar is building a payer-agnostic platform capable of supporting brokers and selling competing carriers’ products. That increases competition for the same enrollment and advisory activity. The positive read-through for eHealth is expansion of the employer-funded individual coverage fee pool and the existence of an identifiable distribution channel, not a demonstrated share gain over Lucie.

Near-term catalysts are employer conversion, active employee enrollment, and disclosure of recurring administration revenue during the 2027 benefit cycle. The longer-duration fundamental shift is a broader market for individual policy selection and benefits administration as employers move toward defined contributions. This opportunity does not resolve eHealth’s capital-structure issues or determine the performance of its larger Medicare-oriented business. An elderly veteran was facing city fines he couldn’t pay because his health left him unable to keep up with the property. No family nearby. Just warning letters and a yard that had gotten away from him. So this guy showed up with his equipment, offered to handle the whole thing at no cost, and started clearing it so the veteran could keep his home.
Minutes later a police officer rolls up, orders him to shut everything down, and tells him if he doesn’t leave he can be arrested. Not for charging money. Not for trespassing. For helping a disabled veteran.
Honestly, this is disappointing as hell from law enforcement. We expect officers to protect people and use common sense, not threaten to cuff someone who’s doing free yard work for a vet the city is already fining. Instead of standing with the veteran or just letting a good deed happen, he chose to escalate a situation that never needed to exist.
When cities can fine disabled veterans for property they physically can’t maintain, then police threaten the people who step in to fix it for free, something’s broken. Veterans who spent their lives serving deserve better than this — and better from the people sworn to protect them.

This is a compilation of findings produced by several large language models independently examining the same topic. The results offer a relatively high degree of credibility and neutrality, and I am sharing them for your reference.

Sources: Nebius official project pages, municipal public FAQs, SEC filings and earnings call transcripts; IREN Q3 FY26 earnings call transcript; Nebius's dedicated project pages for its Missouri and Pennsylvania developments; Nebius Q3 2026 shareholder letter; and IREN FY26 Form 10-K.

Nebius's official definition of an owned site (Greenfield): The land is acquired and owned by Nebius, which leads the design and construction and owns the data center buildings, while also managing the power infrastructure. It is important to note that managing power infrastructure does not necessarily mean owning all the underlying power assets. Ownership of generation facilities, substations and associated electrical infrastructure needs to be assessed on a project-by-project basis.

Nebius has not provided an exact, site-by-site numerical breakdown to substantiate the claim that "more than half of its sites" are owned. It is important to distinguish between the number of owned sites and the proportion of data center capacity that is owned. In its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, Nebius disclosed the proportion of owned facilities within its planned incremental data center capacity: more than 50% of the next 1 GW of capacity, and more than 75% of the subsequent 1 GW. This does not directly establish that more than half of its total site count is owned.

Below are several self-owned projects that Nebius has publicly disclosed individually and for which there is clear supporting project documentation.

I. Independence AI Factory, Missouri

1. Land: In December 2025, Nebius directly acquired approximately 398–400 acres at Eastgate Commerce Center. The land is owned by Nebius. The project will be developed in multiple phases over 5–7 years. The company's current official plan specifies four data center buildings, with a total planned capacity of 1.2 GW.

2. Power structure

800 MW: Electricity will be supplied by the municipal utility, Independence Power and Light. A third-party entity, Independence Power Partners (IPP), a privately held company, is developing a new gas-fired generation facility. Electricity will be delivered into the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) grid, from which Nebius will purchase power. IPP is an independent entity, and the generation facility is not owned by Nebius.

400 MW: Nebius is evaluating an on-site power generation solution. The final technology has not yet been determined, so it cannot be assumed that gas-fired generators will be used, nor should this be treated as a confirmed plan to build Nebius-owned generation assets.

II. Highridge Business Park AI Factory, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania

1. Land: Nebius plans to own approximately 600 acres of land, with the project designed, built and operated under its leadership. The land transactions involve phased acquisitions and conditional purchase arrangements. It would therefore be premature to state that ownership of the entire 600 acres has already been fully transferred.

2. Power: Nebius is working with PPL Electric Utilities to provide electricity and supporting power infrastructure. The project has a total planned capacity of 1.2 GW, with an initial phase of 260 MW targeted to become operational in October 2027.

The project plans include an on-site electrical switchyard and substation, and Nebius has also stated that it will fund relevant power infrastructure upgrades. However, publicly available information is currently insufficient to establish whether these facilities will ultimately be owned by PPL or Nebius. It is therefore not appropriate to conclude that all substations and related electrical infrastructure belong to PPL.

III. Mäntsälä Data Center, Finland

1. Land: Nebius owns the land and built the data center buildings itself. This was Nebius's first wholly owned data center.

2. Power: The facility is connected to the Finnish electricity grid and purchases power through the grid. Current operational capacity is 75 MW, and a GB300 cluster has been deployed. In addition, in October 2026, Nebius signed a contract worth approximately €15 million with Caverion to design and deliver a dedicated substation for its second 70 MW data center. This demonstrates Nebius's involvement in the development of dedicated substation infrastructure, although the ultimate ownership of the facility still requires further verification.

IV. New Lappeenranta AI Factory, Finland

1. Land: The project is located in Pajarila, with a planned total capacity of 310 MW. It will be developed in phases, with the first phase scheduled to become operational in 2027. The project is being advanced through cooperation between Nebius and local partners, involving Polarnode and the local government. Publicly available information is currently insufficient to establish that Nebius has acquired ownership of all the land. It would therefore be premature to describe the entire project as being built on land wholly owned by Nebius.

2. Power: The project will obtain long-term electricity supply through the Finnish grid. There is currently insufficient evidence to establish that the project has its own power generation assets.

Taken together, these projects show that Nebius is actively increasing the proportion of its self-owned data centers. Its Greenfield model encompasses not only land and data center buildings, but also the management of power infrastructure. However, ownership structures for generation facilities, substations and on-site power distribution infrastructure differ across projects and should not be treated as uniform.

What can currently be established is that the Missouri project's 800 MW power supply depends on third-party generation infrastructure and the SPP grid, while the proposed 400 MW of on-site generation remains under evaluation. In Finland, Nebius has initiated the development of a dedicated substation at Mäntsälä. The ownership of the on-site substation infrastructure at the Pennsylvania project still requires further verification.

Therefore, Nebius's self-owned model should not simply be characterized as owning only the land and data center buildings. A more complete assessment needs to examine its actual ownership of power infrastructure, its responsibility for construction, and its degree of operational control.

IREN's owned-site model: IREN acquires and owns the land, leads the design and construction, and owns the data center buildings. It also builds, owns and controls the supporting substations and on-site power distribution infrastructure. The upstream main transmission lines remain the property of the grid operator, while IREN secures electricity through long-term power agreements. It has direct asset ownership and operational control over the critical power infrastructure extending from the substation into the data center.

This represents an important difference between the two companies in the nature of their owned assets and their ability to control critical infrastructure.

Nebius is accelerating the expansion of its self-owned data center capacity and gradually strengthening its ability to manage and develop power infrastructure. IREN, meanwhile, has already integrated land, grid connections, substations, data centers and computing infrastructure into its vertically integrated operating model.

The key question is which company can take control of the critical elements of infrastructure development and operations at a more fundamental level, continuously replicate and scale these capabilities, and ultimately achieve greater efficiency and stronger economics.

text:
O'Keefe v. Read et al Wrongful Death Suit

C.F. McCarthy's has filed a  memorandum responding to the O'Keefe family's opposition to excluding hospitality expert Dr. Marissa Orlowski.

The defense is doubling down on its argument that Orlowski's opinions are irrelevant to the legal standard governing Massachusetts dram shop liability.

And this time, attorneys are pointing to a 2024 Colorado case in which a court excluded similar expert testimony.

HERE'S THE BREAKDOWN:

🔶 1. THE DEFENSE SAYS THE PLAINTIFFS ARE MISSING THE CENTRAL LEGAL ISSUE.

The O'Keefe family argues that even if some of Orlowski's opinions are not directly relevant to summary judgment, her testimony could still assist a jury at trial.

C.F. McCarthy's disagrees.

The defense argues that the issue the plaintiffs characterize as narrow is actually the heart of their claims:

Was Karen Read served alcohol at C.F. McCarthy's while she was visibly intoxicated?

Attorneys contend that Orlowski's opinions do not answer that question because they rely on industry operating standards rather than the applicable legal requirements.

🔶 2. THE DEFENSE CITES A 2024 COLORADO CASE WITH SIMILAR EXPERT TESTIMONY.

C.F. McCarthy's points to Berge v. Su Casa Inc., a Colorado case involving allegations that a bar overserved a patron who subsequently sexually assaulted someone.

In that case, the plaintiff sought to introduce expert testimony concerning alcohol-service regulations, licensing requirements, and operational failures.

However, the Colorado court excluded the expert's opinions.

Why?

According to the decision discussed in McCarthy's filing, the expert relied on negligence-based operating standards that did not match Colorado's applicable dram shop liability standard.

The court also found that such testimony could confuse jurors about what the law actually required.

C.F. McCarthy's argues that the same reasoning should apply to Orlowski.

🔶 3. THE DEFENSE ARGUES THAT POOR BAR PRACTICES DO NOT AUTOMATICALLY ESTABLISH LIABILITY.

The plaintiffs have raised concerns about alcohol-service training, monitoring customers, and the establishments' operating procedures.

But C.F. McCarthy's argues that Massachusetts law does not recognize dram shop liability simply because an establishment allegedly failed to follow industry best practices.

The filing cites Vickowski v. Polish American Citizens Club of Deerfield, emphasizing that a tavern keeper's duty depends on whether the establishment knew or reasonably should have known a patron was intoxicated.

It also cites Homan v. Brandy Barrel Pub & Grill, which addressed the use of a bar's method of operation as a basis for liability.

The defense maintains that the plaintiffs cannot substitute alleged operational deficiencies for evidence satisfying the legal standard.

🔶 4. McCARTHY'S CHALLENGES THE PLAINTIFFS' ARGUMENT ABOUT WHY STAFF FAILED TO OBSERVE INTOXICATION.

The O'Keefe family's opposition argues that Orlowski can explain how alleged operational failures contributed to staff not recognizing signs of intoxication.

C.F. McCarthy's rejects that reasoning.

The defense argues that explaining why bartenders may have failed to observe intoxication is not the same as establishing that Read was visibly intoxicated when served.

Attorneys also contend that the plaintiffs have not identified a Massachusetts case permitting the particular method-of-operation evidence they seek to introduce in this type of dram shop action.

🔶 5. THE DEFENSE SAYS A JURY DOESN'T NEED AN EXPERT TO DETERMINE WHETHER SOMEONE APPEARED INTOXICATED.

This is another major argument.

C.F. McCarthy's cites Commonwealth v. Canty to support its position that ordinary witnesses can offer opinions about whether someone appeared sober or intoxicated.

The defense argues that evaluating visible intoxication is within the understanding of ordinary jurors.

Its position is that expert testimony from Orlowski is unnecessary and could improperly influence the jury's assessment of the evidence.

🔶 6. McCARTHY'S ALSO ADDRESSES THE TIMING OF ITS MOTION.

The plaintiffs previously challenged the timing of the defense's attempt to exclude Orlowski.

In a footnote, C.F. McCarthy's responds that its motion was filed in connection with its summary judgment motion and before the court's deadline for Daubert-Lanigan motions.

The defense also reserves the right to further address expert admissibility issues under the court's trial schedule.

🔶 7. THE DEFENSE WANTS ORLOWSKI EXCLUDED AT EVERY STAGE.

C.F. McCarthy's asks the judge to:

🔷 Strike Orlowski's expert report.

🔷 Refuse to consider her opinions when deciding summary judgment.

🔷Exclude her from offering any expert opinions or testimony at trial.

WHY THIS MATTERS:

This dispute goes beyond whether the bars followed recommended alcohol-service practices.

The central disagreement is whether those practices are legally relevant to proving that C.F. McCarthy's knew or reasonably should have known Karen Read was intoxicated when it served her.

The O'Keefe family argues that Orlowski's expertise can help explain how alleged failures in training and monitoring contributed to intoxication going unnoticed.

C.F. McCarthy's argues that such opinions rely on an improper legal standard and should never reach the jury.

The defense is attempting to draw a very clear distinction between two questions:

🔷Did the bar follow recommended industry practices?

🔷Did the bar know, or should it reasonably have known, that Karen Read was intoxicated when serving her?

Those are not automatically the same question.

And C.F. McCarthy's is arguing that the plaintiffs cannot establish the second merely by criticizing the first.

With Waterfall Bar & Grill also joining the effort to exclude Orlowski, both establishments are now challenging this expert's role in the litigation.

Since the beginning of the generative AI boom, there has been a fight over how large AI models are trained. In one camp sit tech companies such as OpenAI that have claimed it is “impossible” to train AI without hoovering the internet of copyrighted data. And in the other camp are artists who argue that AI companies have taken their intellectual property without consent and compensation. 

Adobe is pretty unusual in that it sides with the latter group, with an  approach that stands out as an example of how generative AI products can be built without scraping copyrighted data from the internet. Adobe released its image-generating model Firefly, which is integrated into its popular photo editing tool Photoshop, one year ago.

In an exclusive interview with MIT Technology Review, Adobe’s AI leaders are adamant this is the only way forward. At stake is not just the livelihood of creators, they say, but our whole information ecosystem. What they have learned shows that building responsible tech doesn’t have to come at the cost of doing business. 

“We worry that the industry, Silicon Valley in particular, does not pause to ask the ‘how’ or the ‘why.’ Just because you can build something doesn’t mean you should build it without consideration of the impact that you’re creating,” says David Wadhwani, president of Adobe’s digital media business. 

Those questions guided the creation of Firefly. When the generative image boom kicked off in 2022, there was a major backlash against AI from creative communities. Many people were using generative AI models as derivative content machines to create images in the style of another artist, sparking a legal fight over copyright and fair use. The latest generative AI technology has also made it much easier to create deepfakes and misinformation. 

It soon became clear that to offer creators proper credit and businesses legal certainty, the company could not build its models by scraping the web of data, Wadwani says.  

Adobe wants to reap the benefits of generative AI while still “recognizing that these are built on the back of human labor. And we have to figure out how to fairly compensate people for that labor now and in the future,” says Ely Greenfield, Adobe’s chief technology officer for digital media.  

To scrape or not to scrape

The scraping of online data, commonplace in AI, has recently become highly controversial. AI companies such as OpenAI, https://t.co/G133p3BVPF, Meta, and Google are facing numerous lawsuits over AI training data. Tech companies argue that publicly available data is fair game. Writers and artists disagree and are pushing for a license-based model, where creators would get compensated for having their work included in training datasets. 

Adobe trained Firefly on content that had an explicit license allowing AI training, which means the bulk of the training data comes from Adobe’s library of stock photos, says Greenfield. The company offers creators extra compensation when material is  used to train AI models, he adds.  

This is in contrast to the status quo in AI today, where tech companies scrape the web indiscriminately and have a limited understanding of what of what the training data includes. Because of these practices, the AI datasets inevitably include copyrighted content and personal data, and research has uncovered toxic content, such as child sexual abuse material. 

Scraping the internet gives tech companies a cheap way to get lots of AI training data, and traditionally, having more data has allowed developers to build more powerful models. Limiting Firefly to licensed data for training was a risky bet, says Greenfield. 

“To be honest, when we started with Firefly with our image model, we didn’t know whether or not we would be able to satisfy customer needs without scraping the web,” says Greenfield. 

“And we found we could, which was great.” 

Human content moderators also review the training data to weed out objectionable or harmful content, known intellectual property, and images of known people, and the company has licenses for everything its products train on. 

Adobe’s strategy has been to integrate generative AI tools into its existing products, says Greenfield. In Photoshop, for example, Firefly users can fill in areas of an image using text commands. This allows them much more control over the creative process, and it aids their creativity. 

Still, more work needs to be done. The company wants to make Firefly even faster. Currently it takes around 10 seconds for the company’s content moderation algorithms to check the outputs of the model, for example, Greenfield says. Adobe is also trying to figure out how some business customers could generate copyrighted content, such as Marvel characters or Mickey Mouse. Adobe has teamed up with companies such as IBM, Mattel, NVIDIA and NASCAR, which allows these companies to use the tool with their intellectual property. It is also working on audio, lip synching tools and  3D generation. 

Garbage in, garbage out

The decision to not scrape the internet also gives Adobe an edge in content moderation. Generative AI is notoriously difficult to control, and developers themselves don’t know why the models generate the images and texts they do. Generative AI models have put out questionable and toxic content in numerous cases. 

That all comes down to what it has been trained on, Greenfield says. He says Adobe’s model has never seen a picture of Joe Biden or Donald Trump, for example, and it cannot be coaxed into generating political misinformation. The AI model’s training data has no news content or famous people. It has not been trained on any copyrighted material, such as images of Mickey Mouse. 

“It just doesn’t understand what that concept is,” says Greenfield. 

Adobe also applies automated content moderation at the point of creation to check that Firefly’s creations are safe for professional use. The model is prohibited from creating news stories or violent images. Some names of artists are also blocked. Firefly-generated content comes with labels that indicate it has been created using AI, and the image’s edit history. 

During a critical election year, the need to know who made a piece of content, and how, is especially important. Adobe has been a vocal advocate for labels on AI content that tell where it originated, and with whom. 

The company started the Content Authenticity Initiative, an association promoting the use of labels which tell you whether content is AI-generated or not, along with the New York Times and Twitter (now X). The initiative now has over 2,500 members. It is also part of developing C2PA, an industry standard label which shows where a piece of content has come from, and how it was created. 

“We’re long overdue [for] a better education in media literacy and tools that support people’s ability to validate any content that claims to represent reality,” Greenfield says. 

Adobe’s approach highlights the need for AI companies to be thinking deeply about content moderation, says Claire Leibowicz, head of AI and media integrity at the nonprofit Partnership on AI. 

Adobe’s approach toward generative AI serves those societal goals by fighting misinformation as well as promoting business goals, such as preserving creator autonomy and attribution, adds Leibowicz. 

“The business mission of Adobe is not to prevent misinformation, per se,” she says. “It’s to empower creators. And isn’t this a really elegant confluence of mission and tactics, to be able to kill two birds with one stone?” 

Wadhwani agrees. The company says Firefly-powered features are among its most popular, and 90% of Firefly’s web app users are entirely new customers to Adobe. 

 “I think our approach has definitely been good for business,” Wadhwani says.

Microsoft’s newly published patent for a "distributed GPU computing network" has many people asking: Isn't this literally what Pi Network is already doing?

On the surface, both tell the same story: pooling idle consumer hardware worldwide to build a decentralized AI compute network. 
Under the hood, however, they are playing two completely different games 👇

1️⃣ Hardware Core: Heavyweight GPUs vs. Lightweight CPUs
🔹 Microsoft Patent: Targets dedicated GPUs inside gaming PCs and laptops. It breaks down massive AI model training into smaller chunks, relying on raw parallel computing power.
🔹 Pi Network: Mobile users simply tap daily for consensus, while desktop Pi Nodes run Docker-based CPU containers for network validation and lightweight AI inference (like basic image recognition)—nowhere near the compute scale of training large models.

2️⃣ Business Loop: B2B Fiat Payouts vs. Web3 Tokenomics
🔹 Microsoft (Web2 Giant): Backed by Azure’s massive enterprise clientele, compute demand is real and immediate. Users contribute GPU power and get paid directly in cash or cloud credits.
🔹 Pi (Web3 / DePIN): Relies on native token incentives, meaning real-world value depends heavily on secondary market liquidity and external demand.

3️⃣ Security Moat: Enterprise Sandboxing vs. Public Networks
Companies won't train proprietary models on consumer PCs without ironclad privacy. A major focus of Microsoft's patent is cryptographic isolation and sandboxing to protect sensitive corporate data—the exact assurance needed to land enterprise deals.

💡 Takeaway:
Similar vision, vastly different scale. A tech giant entering this space validates "distributed compute" as a major future trend and reinforces the broader narrative for the sector.

⚠️ Scam Alert: This is strictly a patent filing—Microsoft has NOT released any official GPU mining or earning app. Any link claiming to offer "official Microsoft GPU mining" right now is 100% malware/scam. Stay safe!

One of the group struggled at first with the classic human reflex: the need to manage, to stay in control, to analyze instead of surrender. We stayed close, offering only the lightest verbal anchors. Each time he edged closer to release, the medicine met him with patience rather than force. Slowly the grip loosened. Eventually he dropped fully, and the relief that followed was almost audible in the room.
Another carried a long habit of emotional control. The medicine did not negotiate. It met him face-to-face, and the confrontation was honest. He purged—clean, purposeful, necessary—and on the other side of that release found a state of pure experiencing that required no commentary, no defense, no story. Just presence.
Throughout both the morning and afternoon sessions, the lasers remained available as an optional doorway into the particular visual phenomena Goler and others have described—the recurring geometric structures and code-like symbols that appear within the diffracted light. Some chose to engage that exploration; others remained fully immersed in the inner landscapes the medicine itself presented. Either way, the container stayed the same: careful, non-directive, and devoted entirely to personal discovery.
What became clear, again, is that deep medicine is not always about receiving concise answers, tidy information, or clear instruction from the other side. Sometimes the molecule seems to laugh at our direct questions. It refuses to hand over a neat download and instead points us back toward the slower, more ordinary work of connecting—with ourselves, with one another, with the texture of daily life—and discovering the answers that can only be found by living them. The real gift is often the capacity it restores: the ability to listen inward, to trust what arises in the quiet of terrestrial experience, and to keep doing the work long after the session ends.
In the end, the depth of any such journey remains profoundly subjective. No one standing outside it can measure its value or declare its meaning. Only the one who walked it can know what it offered, what it asked, and what it ultimately revealed.
The room itself seemed to breathe with them. Connection moved in every direction: connection to self, yes, but also to the people sharing the space, to the quiet clink of a water glass later, to the cultural threads each person carried, to the shifting perceptions that make ordinary reality feel newly transparent. Psychedelic medicines have a way of dissolving the usual filters so that understanding can arrive not as theory but as direct knowing. In scientific language we might speak of temporary shifts in default-mode network activity, increased neural entropy, or enhanced binding of serotonin receptors. In the language of the experience itself, it simply feels like the universe deciding to show you a few more of its cards—and then sitting with you while you decide what to do with them.
We were not offering therapy that day. We were offering a carefully held container for people who already knew how to meet themselves. The medicine did the rest. And when the final session softened and the gongs spoke one last time, the seven of us remained for a while in the quiet afterglow—feet still pointed toward the center, hearts a little more open than when we had begun.

Your distinction between “Islam” and “Muslims” is the standard defensive move, but it does not hold up well against the primary sources or the historical record. The Quran, Hadith, and classical jurisprudence do not merely tolerate conquest, slavery, and subordination of non-Muslims as unfortunate human failings; they regulate and in important respects endorse them.

The early expansions that created what became the Arab world were military campaigns framed as jihad. Non-Muslims were typically offered conversion, the jizya (a poll tax imposed on the subjugated while they remained in a state of “humiliation,” per Quran 9:29 and the classical commentaries), or the sword. Captives were enslaved as a matter of course. This is not an external “political” overlay; it is how the tradition itself describes the process. The same sources that praise freeing slaves as a meritorious act (and they do) also permit ownership, sexual use of female captives, and the buying and selling of human beings. Muhammad owned slaves and took captives as wives/concubines. Manumission as piety is not the same as abolition of the institution.
The Arab/Muslim slave trade operated for roughly thirteen centuries—far longer than the Atlantic trade—and estimates put the numbers of Africans alone in the multi-millions (commonly cited ranges of 10–17 million, plus Europeans and others). It was suppressed in large part by British naval power in the 19th century, after Britain had already moved against its own earlier involvement in the Atlantic trade. That fact does not vanish because the British Empire also had colonial sins. Pointing at British or American history is whataboutism; it does not rewrite the Islamic legal and historical record on slavery or conquest. Slavery has not disappeared in every Muslim-majority society either. 

Hereditary slavery persists in Mauritania among Arab-Berber and other communities; trafficking and forced labour continue in places such as Libya. These are not fringe anomalies unrelated to long-standing social patterns.
On the double-standard point: yes, Christians and Jews have done terrible things, and Christian societies eventually generated strong internal abolitionist movements that successfully argued against practices that had biblical precedents. Islam has not produced an equivalent successful doctrinal reformation that removes the permission for jihadist expansion, the classical rules on dhimmis, or the permissibility of slavery. Large majorities in many Muslim-majority countries still want some form of sharia as official or influential law. 

Derived figures from the 2013 Pew survey show substantial support (often majorities or large minorities in places such as Egypt, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Jordan, and the Palestinian territories) for the death penalty for apostasy among those who favour sharia, and non-trivial minorities for hudud corporal punishments. Support for violence “in defence of Islam” has declined from earlier peaks in many places but remains double-digit in several countries and territories.
