⛵ CHRISTOPHER COLUMBUS: THE VOYAGES THAT CHANGED THE WORLD, IN 250 FACTS

🧭 BEFORE THE VOYAGE
𝟏. Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa, Italy, probably in 1451

𝟐. In Italian he was Cristoforo Colombo, and in Spain Cristóbal Colón

𝟑. His father Domenico was a wool weaver

𝟒. He went to sea as a teenager, trading around the Mediterranean

𝟓. In 1476 his ship was sunk in a battle off Portugal, and he swam ashore, reportedly clinging to an oar

𝟔. He settled in Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew worked as a mapmaker

𝟕. He sailed as far north as Ireland and, he claimed, Iceland

𝟖. He also sailed south to the Portuguese fort of Elmina on Africa's Gold Coast

𝟗. Around 1479 he married Filipa Moniz Perestrelo, from a noble family linked to the Madeira islands

𝟏𝟎. Their son Diego was born around 1480

𝟏𝟏. He read Marco Polo's travels and filled his books with notes about the riches of Asia

𝟏𝟐. Like all educated Europeans of his day, he knew the Earth was round. The "flat Earth" story is a myth

𝟏𝟑. His real mistake was size: he thought Japan lay about 4,000 km west of the Canary Islands. The true distance is nearly 20,000 km

𝟏𝟒. He was encouraged by a letter and map from the Florentine scholar Toscanelli

𝟏𝟓. Around 1485 King John II of Portugal turned his plan down on his experts' advice

𝟏𝟔. After Filipa died, he moved to Spain with young Diego

𝟏𝟕. Friars at the monastery of La Rábida, near the port of Palos, took them in and backed his plan

𝟏𝟖. In 1486 he first pitched his idea to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand

𝟏𝟗. A royal commission rejected it, saying his distances were wrong. They were right

𝟐𝟎. While he waited, the Crown paid him a small allowance

𝟐𝟏. In 1488 his second son, Fernando, was born to Beatriz Enríquez de Arana

𝟐𝟐. His brother Bartholomew tried to win backing from the kings of England and France

𝟐𝟑. Columbus waited about six years for a Spanish yes

𝟐𝟒. In January 1492 Spain captured Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, freeing the monarchs to look further afield

𝟐𝟓. Rejected once more, Columbus rode away, but a royal messenger caught up with him and called him back

𝟐𝟔. The royal treasurer Luis de Santángel persuaded the Queen and helped raise the money

𝟐𝟕. The famous story that Isabella pawned her jewels to pay for the voyage is a myth

𝟐𝟖. On 17 April 1492 the Capitulations of Santa Fe made him "Admiral of the Ocean Sea" and viceroy of any lands he found

𝟐𝟗. He was also promised 10% of all the riches from those lands

𝟑𝟎. The town of Palos was ordered to provide two ships as a punishment for an offence against the Crown

𝟑𝟏. The respected Pinzón brothers, Martín Alonso and Vicente Yáñez, persuaded local sailors to sign up

⛵ THE FIRST VOYAGE (1492–1493)
𝟑𝟐. Three ships set out: the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña

𝟑𝟑. The Santa María was a heavy cargo ship, while the Pinta and Niña were fast, light caravels

𝟑𝟒. The Niña's real name was the Santa Clara. "Niña" was a nickname from her owner, Juan Niño

𝟑𝟓. The Santa María belonged to Juan de la Cosa, who later drew the oldest surviving map showing the Americas

𝟑𝟔. Martín Alonso Pinzón captained the Pinta, and his brother Vicente Yáñez the Niña

𝟑𝟕. About 90 men sailed, almost all experienced sailors from southern Spain

𝟑𝟖. Only four were convicts, pardoned in exchange for joining

𝟑𝟗. An interpreter, Luis de Torres, who spoke Hebrew and Arabic, came along to talk to the "Great Khan" of China

𝟒𝟎. There was no priest on board

𝟒𝟏. They sailed from Palos at dawn on 3 August 1492

𝟒𝟐. Days earlier, the deadline for Spain's Jews to convert or leave the country had expired

𝟒𝟑. Their first stop was the Canary Islands, Spain's last outpost in the Atlantic

𝟒𝟒. The Pinta's rudder broke soon after leaving, and Columbus suspected her owners of sabotage

𝟒𝟓. In the Canaries, the Niña's triangular sails were swapped for square ones to run before the wind

𝟒𝟔. They took on water, firewood and food on the island of La Gomera

𝟒𝟕. On 6 September 1492 they left La Gomera and sailed into the unknown

𝟒𝟖. Columbus kept two logs: a secret true one, and one with shorter distances to stop the crew panicking about how far from home they were

𝟒𝟗. Ironically, the "fake" figures were closer to the truth, because he overestimated his speed

𝟓𝟎. The steady trade winds pushed them west day after day

𝟓𝟏. On 13 September the compass needles drifted from the North Star, alarming the pilots

𝟓𝟐. On 15 September a great meteor fell into the sea

𝟓𝟑. Later in September they entered the Sargasso Sea, so full of floating seaweed that sailors feared running aground

𝟓𝟒. Birds, seaweed and whales raised false hopes of land again and again

𝟓𝟓. On 25 September Martín Alonso Pinzón shouted "Land!" The crew sang a hymn, but it was only clouds

𝟓𝟔. By early October the crew was close to mutiny

𝟓𝟕. On 7 October Columbus changed course to the west-southwest, following flocks of migrating birds

𝟓𝟖. On 10 October, according to some accounts, he promised to turn back if land was not found within days

𝟓𝟗. On 11 October they fished out a carved stick and a branch with berries

𝟔𝟎. That night Columbus said he saw a light "like a small wax candle" rising and falling in the distance

𝟔𝟏. At about 2 a.m. on 12 October 1492, Rodrigo de Triana, a lookout on the Pinta, cried "¡Tierra!"

𝟔𝟐. The Crown had promised a pension of 10,000 maravedís a year to the first to see land

𝟔𝟑. Columbus kept the reward himself, claiming he had seen the light first

𝟔𝟒. The crossing from the Canaries had taken about five weeks

𝟔𝟓. They landed on an island in the Bahamas that its Taíno people called Guanahani

𝟔𝟔. Columbus renamed it San Salvador, "Holy Saviour"

𝟔𝟕. Exactly which island it was is still debated. In 1925 the Bahamas renamed Watling Island as San Salvador

𝟔𝟖. He went ashore with the royal banner and claimed the island for Spain

𝟔𝟗. The Taíno greeted them peacefully, offering parrots, balls of cotton thread and spears

𝟕𝟎. In his log Columbus wrote that they would make good servants and could easily be converted

𝟕𝟏. He saw small gold rings in their noses and asked where the gold came from

𝟕𝟐. He took several Taíno captive to guide him through the islands

𝟕𝟑. He called the people "Indians" because he believed he had reached the Indies

𝟕𝟒. On 28 October he reached Cuba, which he believed was part of mainland Asia

𝟕𝟓. He sent Luis de Torres and another man inland to find the Great Khan. They found a village of thatched huts

𝟕𝟔. There the envoys saw people smoking rolled leaves: Europeans' first meeting with tobacco

𝟕𝟕. The Spaniards also saw people sleeping in hammocks. The word comes from the Taíno language

𝟕𝟖. On 21 November Martín Alonso Pinzón sailed off in the Pinta without permission to hunt for gold

𝟕𝟗. On 6 December Columbus reached a large island he named La Española: Hispaniola

𝟖𝟎. There he met the Taíno chief Guacanagarí, who became his ally

𝟖𝟏. On Christmas Eve 1492, while Columbus slept, a ship's boy at the helm ran the Santa María onto a reef

𝟖𝟐. Guacanagarí's people helped unload the cargo, and Columbus noted that not a single item went missing

𝟖𝟑. From the wreck's timbers the men built a fort, La Navidad, "Christmas"

𝟖𝟒. Columbus left 39 men there: the first European settlement in the Americas since the Vikings

𝟖𝟓. On 4 January 1493 he set sail for home in the Niña

𝟖𝟔. Two days later the Pinta rejoined him. Pinzón had found gold

𝟖𝟕. On 13 January, in a bay on Hispaniola, the Spaniards fought Indigenous archers. Columbus named it the Bay of Arrows

𝟖𝟖. He carried several Taíno captives back to Spain

𝟖𝟗. On 14 February 1493 a violent storm separated the two ships

𝟗𝟎. Sure he would die, Columbus wrote an account of his discovery, sealed it in a barrel and threw it into the sea. It was never found

𝟗𝟏. The crew drew lots with chickpeas, one marked with a cross, to choose who would make a pilgrimage if they survived. Columbus drew the cross

𝟗𝟐. They reached the Azores, where Portuguese officials arrested half the crew as they went ashore to pray

𝟗𝟑. Another storm forced Columbus into Lisbon, the capital of Spain's great rival, on 4 March 1493

𝟗𝟒. King John II of Portugal received him and claimed the new lands might be his

𝟗𝟓. On 15 March 1493 the Niña sailed into Palos, and the Pinta arrived on the very same day

𝟗𝟔. Martín Alonso Pinzón died within weeks, sick and exhausted

𝟗𝟕. Columbus's letter describing his discovery was printed and spread across Europe within months

𝟗𝟖. In Barcelona Isabella and Ferdinand received him as a hero

𝟗𝟗. He paraded Taíno people, parrots and gold before the court

𝟏𝟎𝟎. Six of the Taíno were baptised, with the King and Queen as godparents

𝟏𝟎𝟏. The famous "egg of Columbus" story, in which he makes an egg stand by cracking its end, is probably a legend

𝟏𝟎𝟐. In May 1493 Pope Alexander VI drew a line through the Atlantic, giving lands to its west to Spain

𝟏𝟎𝟑. In 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas moved the line further west. That is why Brazil speaks Portuguese today

🏝️ THE SECOND VOYAGE (1493–1496)
𝟏𝟎𝟒. This time he sailed with 17 ships and about 1,200 men

𝟏𝟎𝟓. It was a colonising fleet, carrying settlers, soldiers, priests and craftsmen

𝟏𝟎𝟔. The ships carried horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, wheat and sugar cane, which would transform the Americas

𝟏𝟎𝟕. They left Cádiz on 25 September 1493

𝟏𝟎𝟖. The crossing from the Canaries took only about three weeks

𝟏𝟎𝟗. On 3 November 1493 he sighted an island he named Dominica, because it was a Sunday

𝟏𝟏𝟎. He named Guadeloupe after a famous monastery in Spain

𝟏𝟏𝟏. On Guadeloupe the Spaniards reported finding signs of cannibalism among the Carib people

𝟏𝟏𝟐. The word "cannibal" comes from Carib, the name Europeans gave these islanders

𝟏𝟏𝟑. Sailing north, he named Montserrat, Antigua and many other islands

𝟏𝟏𝟒. At St Croix, Spaniards and Caribs fought the first recorded battle between Europeans and Indigenous people in the Caribbean

𝟏𝟏𝟓. He named the Virgin Islands after Saint Ursula and her legendary 11,000 virgins

𝟏𝟏𝟔. On 19 November 1493 he reached Puerto Rico, which he called San Juan Bautista

𝟏𝟏𝟕. On 28 November he reached La Navidad and found it burned to the ground

𝟏𝟏𝟖. All 39 men he had left behind were dead

𝟏𝟏𝟗. The Taíno said the settlers had fought among themselves over gold and women and were killed by the chief Caonabo

𝟏𝟐𝟎. In January 1494 Columbus founded La Isabela on Hispaniola, the first planned European town in the Americas

𝟏𝟐𝟏. Soon after, the first recorded Catholic Mass in the Americas was held there

𝟏𝟐𝟐. The settlers fell ill with fevers, and many died

𝟏𝟐𝟑. Columbus sent 12 ships home, begging Spain for food and medicine

𝟏𝟐𝟒. He sent soldiers inland to the Cibao valley to find gold and built a fort there

𝟏𝟐𝟓. In April 1494 he set off to explore Cuba and Jamaica

𝟏𝟐𝟔. In May 1494 he reached Jamaica, which he called Santiago

𝟏𝟐𝟕. Sailing along Cuba's south coast, he made his crew swear an oath that Cuba was a continent, not an island

𝟏𝟐𝟖. Anyone who later said otherwise faced a fine, and sailors were threatened with having their tongues cut out

𝟏𝟐𝟗. Returning exhausted, he fell gravely ill and was unconscious for days

𝟏𝟑𝟎. His brother Bartholomew arrived on Hispaniola to help him rule

𝟏𝟑𝟏. The settlers' raids for food, gold and women drove the Taíno to revolt

𝟏𝟑𝟐. In 1495 Spanish soldiers with horses and war dogs crushed a Taíno army in the Vega Real valley

𝟏𝟑𝟑. Columbus imposed a tribute: every Taíno over 14 had to hand over a small bell full of gold dust every three months

𝟏𝟑𝟒. Those who failed faced harsh punishment

𝟏𝟑𝟓. In 1495 he shipped about 500 Taíno to Spain as slaves. Some 200 died on the voyage

𝟏𝟑𝟔. Queen Isabella later questioned the trade and ordered some of the enslaved Taíno freed and sent home

𝟏𝟑𝟕. The chief Caonabo was captured, reportedly tricked into wearing shiny handcuffs as if they were royal bracelets. He died on the way to Spain

𝟏𝟑𝟖. In 1495 a hurricane wrecked ships in La Isabela's harbour, one of the first hurricanes recorded by Europeans

𝟏𝟑𝟗. The word "hurricane" comes from the Taíno word hurakán

𝟏𝟒𝟎. From the wrecks the Spaniards built the India, the first European ship built in the Americas

𝟏𝟒𝟏. Complaints about Columbus's rule reached Spain, and the Crown sent an investigator, Juan Aguado

𝟏𝟒𝟐. In March 1496 Columbus sailed home to defend himself, leaving Bartholomew in charge

𝟏𝟒𝟑. Food ran so low on the way home that, according to his son, some sailors proposed eating the Taíno captives. Columbus refused

𝟏𝟒𝟒. In June 1496 he reached Cádiz wearing the plain brown habit of a Franciscan friar

𝟏𝟒𝟓. His brother Bartholomew founded Santo Domingo, now the oldest European-founded city still standing in the Americas

🌊 THE THIRD VOYAGE (1498–1500)
𝟏𝟒𝟔. It took two years to raise money and men for a third voyage

𝟏𝟒𝟕. Few volunteers wanted to go, so convicts were offered pardons to join

𝟏𝟒𝟖. On 30 May 1498 he sailed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda with six ships

𝟏𝟒𝟗. He sent three ships straight to Hispaniola and took the other three further south than ever before

𝟏𝟓𝟎. Near the equator the wind died, and the heat was so fierce that the food and wine spoiled

𝟏𝟓𝟏. On 31 July 1498 a sailor spotted three peaks, and Columbus named the island Trinidad, after the Holy Trinity

𝟏𝟓𝟐. On 1 August 1498 he saw the coast of South America for the first time

𝟏𝟓𝟑. On 5 August his men landed on the Paria peninsula in Venezuela. Columbus, suffering from an eye infection, stayed on board

𝟏𝟓𝟒. It was the first recorded European landing on the South American mainland

𝟏𝟓𝟓. He saw the Orinoco River pour so much fresh water into the sea that it must drain "a very great continent"

𝟏𝟓𝟔. He wrote that it was "another world", yet he still believed it lay near Asia

𝟏𝟓𝟕. He even suggested the Garden of Eden lay nearby

𝟏𝟓𝟖. He also claimed the Earth was not a perfect sphere but shaped like a pear

𝟏𝟓𝟗. He named the dangerous straits around Trinidad the Serpent's Mouth and the Dragon's Mouth

𝟏𝟔𝟎. Half-blind and crippled by arthritis, he headed for Hispaniola

𝟏𝟔𝟏. On 31 August 1498 he reached Santo Domingo

𝟏𝟔𝟐. He found the colony in open revolt, led by the former mayor Francisco Roldán

𝟏𝟔𝟑. To make peace, he gave the rebels land and the forced labour of Indigenous people

𝟏𝟔𝟒. He also had several rebels hanged

𝟏𝟔𝟓. Settlers who returned to Spain complained bitterly about the Columbus brothers

𝟏𝟔𝟔. In 1500 the Crown sent a new judge, Francisco de Bobadilla, with full powers

𝟏𝟔𝟕. When Bobadilla arrived in August 1500, Spaniards' bodies were hanging from the gallows

𝟏𝟔𝟖. He arrested Columbus and his brothers

𝟏𝟔𝟗. In October 1500 Columbus was sent back to Spain in chains

𝟏𝟕𝟎. The ship's captain offered to remove the chains, but Columbus refused until the King and Queen ordered it

𝟏𝟕𝟏. According to his son, he kept the chains for the rest of his life and wanted to be buried with them

𝟏𝟕𝟐. In 2006 historians publicised Bobadilla's long-lost report, full of witness accounts of the brothers' brutal rule

𝟏𝟕𝟑. In December 1500 the monarchs freed him and received him at the Alhambra in Granada

𝟏𝟕𝟒. They restored his wealth, but not his power as governor

𝟏𝟕𝟓. Nicolás de Ovando was sent to govern Hispaniola in his place

𝟏𝟕𝟔. Meanwhile Portugal's Vasco da Gama had reached India by sailing around Africa in 1498

𝟏𝟕𝟕. In 1500 the Portuguese explorer Cabral landed in Brazil

𝟏𝟕𝟖. Amerigo Vespucci, who sailed along South America, argued it was a "New World"

𝟏𝟕𝟗. In 1507 a German map named the new continent "America" after Vespucci, not Columbus

𝟏𝟖𝟎. Back in Spain, Columbus wrote a Book of Prophecies, arguing his voyages fulfilled the Bible

⚓ THE FOURTH VOYAGE (1502–1504)
𝟏𝟖𝟏. He called his last journey "the High Voyage"

𝟏𝟖𝟐. His goal was to find a sea passage through the new lands to the Indian Ocean

𝟏𝟖𝟑. On 11 May 1502 he left Cádiz with four ships and about 140 men

𝟏𝟖𝟒. His 13-year-old son Fernando sailed with him

𝟏𝟖𝟓. He was forbidden to stop at Hispaniola

𝟏𝟖𝟔. The crossing took just 21 days, his fastest ever

𝟏𝟖𝟕. In June 1502 he anchored off Santo Domingo anyway, warned that a hurricane was coming and asked for shelter

𝟏𝟖𝟖. Governor Ovando refused to let him in and ignored his warning

𝟏𝟖𝟗. A treasure fleet of about 30 ships sailed for Spain anyway

𝟏𝟗𝟎. The hurricane sank around 20 of them, drowning some 500 men, including Bobadilla and the rebel Roldán

𝟏𝟗𝟏. The one ship that reached Spain carried Columbus's own share of the gold

𝟏𝟗𝟐. His own ships, sheltering in a nearby bay, survived

𝟏𝟗𝟑. In July 1502 he reached the island of Guanaja off Honduras

𝟏𝟗𝟒. There he met a huge trading canoe, as long as a galley and about 2.4 m wide, with some 25 paddlers

𝟏𝟗𝟓. It carried cotton cloth, copper tools and cacao beans, probably from the Maya world

𝟏𝟗𝟔. The traders treated cacao beans as money: when some were dropped, his son wrote, they stooped to pick them up as if they had lost their eyes

𝟏𝟗𝟕. For about a month he battled east along the coast of Honduras against wind, rain and current

𝟏𝟗𝟖. When the coast finally turned south, he named the point Cape Gracias a Dios: "Thanks be to God"

𝟏𝟗𝟗. He sailed on along the coasts of Nicaragua and Costa Rica

𝟐𝟎𝟎. Local people told him of another sea just a few days' walk away. It was the Pacific

𝟐𝟎𝟏. He never found a way through, unaware how close the Pacific was

𝟐𝟎𝟐. Off Panama he found gold and heard of rich mines in Veragua

𝟐𝟎𝟑. Around Christmas 1502 savage storms hit the fleet, and a waterspout passed close by. Columbus read from the Gospel of John to ward it off

𝟐𝟎𝟒. In January 1503 he founded Santa María de Belén in Panama, the first attempted European settlement on the American mainland

𝟐𝟎𝟓. The local chief, Quibián, attacked, and the settlement was abandoned in April 1503

𝟐𝟎𝟔. Feverish and alone, Columbus wrote that he heard a heavenly voice comforting him

𝟐𝟎𝟕. Shipworms had riddled the hulls with holes, and two ships had to be abandoned

𝟐𝟎𝟖. With two leaking ships left, he tried to reach Hispaniola but could not

𝟐𝟎𝟗. On 25 June 1503 he ran both ships aground on Jamaica's north coast

𝟐𝟏𝟎. He and his men were stranded there for a year

𝟐𝟏𝟏. His loyal officer Diego Méndez paddled a dugout canoe across open sea to Hispaniola to fetch help

𝟐𝟏𝟐. Some of the Taíno paddlers died of thirst on the crossing

𝟐𝟏𝟑. Governor Ovando left Columbus stranded for months before sending a rescue ship

𝟐𝟏𝟒. In January 1504 about half the men mutinied under the Porras brothers and set off on their own

𝟐𝟏𝟓. The local Taíno grew tired of feeding the Spaniards and stopped bringing food

𝟐𝟏𝟔. Columbus had an almanac predicting a total lunar eclipse on 29 February 1504

𝟐𝟏𝟕. He told the Taíno chiefs that God was angry and would make the moon "inflamed with wrath"

𝟐𝟏𝟖. When the moon turned blood red, the terrified Taíno begged him to intercede, and the food came back

𝟐𝟏𝟗. In May 1504 his loyal men, led by his brother Bartholomew, defeated the mutineers

𝟐𝟐𝟎. In June 1504 a rescue ship finally arrived

𝟐𝟐𝟏. On 7 November 1504 he reached Spain. He never sailed again

⚰️ HIS LAST YEARS AND LEGACY
𝟐𝟐𝟐. On 26 November 1504 Queen Isabella, his greatest supporter, died

𝟐𝟐𝟑. He spent his final months begging King Ferdinand to restore his titles and income

𝟐𝟐𝟒. Contrary to legend, he did not die poor. He lived comfortably on his share of the gold

𝟐𝟐𝟓. He died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506, aged about 54

𝟐𝟐𝟔. Most historians believe he died still convinced he had reached Asia

𝟐𝟐𝟕. His remains travelled further after death than many people do in life: Valladolid, Seville, Santo Domingo, Havana and back to Seville

𝟐𝟐𝟖. The Dominican Republic still says it holds his bones in a giant monument in Santo Domingo

𝟐𝟐𝟗. DNA tests show at least some of the remains in Seville Cathedral are his

𝟐𝟑𝟎. In 2024 a Spanish documentary claimed DNA showed he was of Sephardic Jewish origin. Other scientists disputed it

𝟐𝟑𝟏. His son Diego later became governor of Hispaniola

𝟐𝟑𝟐. His son Fernando built one of Europe's largest libraries, with more than 15,000 books

𝟐𝟑𝟑. Fernando also wrote a biography of his father

𝟐𝟑𝟒. The original log of the first voyage is lost. We know it from a summary by the friar Bartolomé de las Casas

𝟐𝟑𝟓. Las Casas also became one of the fiercest critics of how the Spanish treated Indigenous people

𝟐𝟑𝟔. His heirs fought the Spanish Crown in court over his rights for decades

𝟐𝟑𝟕. Within decades of his arrival, Hispaniola's Taíno population collapsed from disease, war and forced labour

𝟐𝟑𝟖. The swap of plants, animals and diseases that followed is known as the Columbian Exchange

𝟐𝟑𝟗. Europe gained maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cacao and tobacco

𝟐𝟒𝟎. The Americas gained horses, cattle, pigs, wheat and sugar cane, and also smallpox and measles

𝟐𝟒𝟏. He was not the first European to reach the Americas: Norse sailors reached Newfoundland about 500 years earlier

𝟐𝟒𝟐. He never set foot on the mainland of what is now the United States

𝟐𝟒𝟑. He crossed the Atlantic eight times in all

𝟐𝟒𝟒. No trace of the Santa María has ever been found. A 2014 claim to have found the wreck was rejected by UNESCO experts

𝟐𝟒𝟓. Colombia, British Columbia and Columbus, Ohio, are all named after him

𝟐𝟒𝟔. Columbus Day became a US national holiday in 1937

𝟐𝟒𝟕. Spain celebrates its National Day on 12 October, the day of his landfall

𝟐𝟒𝟖. Many places now mark Indigenous Peoples' Day instead of Columbus Day

𝟐𝟒𝟗. In 2020 several statues of him were toppled or removed in US cities

𝟐𝟓𝟎. More than 500 years on, his voyages are seen as the start of both globalisation and centuries of colonial conquest

text:
My cousin works in the front office of a professional baseball team in Japan.

Every season, the team evaluates its foreign players on a standard form. Eight categories. The form was designed in 1987 and has never been changed. It was built to answer one question: will this American cause problems?

This year's American is a catcher from Oklahoma. Thirty-three. Slightly wider than our dugout door. Let's call him Lane.

My cousin let me translate his form.

1. PUNCTUALITY
Arrives two hours before every game. Not to train. To learn the names of the stadium staff. All 140 of them. He knows the parking attendant's daughter is applying to nursing school. We did not know this.

2. RESPECT FOR SENIORITY
Calls the 68-year-old groundskeeper "Mr. Enomoto, sir." Calls the team owner "Chief." Calls the owner's 91-year-old mother "young lady." She has attended every home game since.

3. TEAM HARMONY
Started a barbecue in the players' parking lot after every home win. Our backup shortstop, 22, has not spoken in a team meeting in three seasons. He now runs the grill. He has opinions about ribs. He shares them.

4. EMOTIONAL RESTRAINT
In August, our rookie hit his first walk-off home run. The first player out of the dugout was Lane. Crying. He was not involved in the play. He was involved emotionally.

5. LANGUAGE EFFORT
Speaks 41 words of Japanese. 30 are food. Says "arigato" to the umpire after strike three. The umpires held a meeting about this. They have decided they like it.

6. FAN RELATIONS
Signs every autograph. Every single one. After a loss in July, he stayed two hours in the rain. A security guard held an umbrella over him. A second guard held an umbrella over the first guard. A third guard went for coffee.

7. CONDUCT TOWARD OPPONENTS
Tipped his cap to a pitcher who struck him out. The pitcher's mother wrote us a letter. We have no procedure for this letter. It is in a drawer.

8. ADDITIONAL REMARKS
Our rookie is Kaisei. He is 20. His father had not missed a home game since Kaisei signed. Three hours each way. Section 14, row 3. He always brought the same banner, made from an old tablecloth, with Kaisei's name painted on it in big, shaky letters.

In June, his father died suddenly.

Lane does not understand Buddhist funerals. He went anyway. He bought a black suit that morning. It was the biggest one in the store, and it was still too small. He took the last seat in the last row.

When it was his turn to offer incense, he froze. He didn't know how.

Kaisei's little brother, who is nine, came down the aisle to the last row, took Lane's huge hand, and showed him. Pinch. Lift to the forehead. Drop. Bow.

Lane did it exactly the way he was taught. Then he stayed for all three hours.

At the end, he gave Kaisei his bat. The one he hit his first home run in Japan with.

"Your dad's got a better view than any of us now," he said. "Every at-bat. Let's give him something to watch."

The next home game, there was something new hanging in our dugout. An old tablecloth. Kaisei's name in big, shaky letters.

Lane had asked the family if he could borrow it. He hung it himself before every game until the season ended. Nobody told him to.

Kaisei batted .310 from June on. With that bat.

The walk-off in August, the one Lane cried about? That was Kaisei. That was the bat. Rounding third, Kaisei pointed at the dugout. Not at the crowd. At the tablecloth.

The form ends with one last box. RECOMMEND CONTRACT RENEWAL: YES / NO.

For 39 years, the general manager has circled one word and filed it.

This year, somebody turned the form over.

Twenty-eight signatures. The entire roster. The backup shortstop. Kaisei, in very large letters. Mr. Enomoto, the groundskeeper, who is not on the roster and was not asked. A very careful pencil signature from a nine-year-old, who is also not on the roster. And Kaisei's mother, who mailed hers in a separate envelope and asked that it please be stapled on.

Under all of them, one word in English, in the groundskeeper's handwriting:

"PLEASE."

Lane signed for two more years.

The form has still never been changed. But my cousin says that next season, they're adding a ninth category.

America, you sent us a catcher.
